The stone scoop in his hand glowed with a sick green sheen as licklets of ﬂame darted over the surface of the viscous liquid it contained.  ‘Drink up! Hyeh heh heh,’ the demon’s throaty chortle kept going despite being drowned in volume by her screams. His bird-claw hand held the scoop with practised steadiness as he poured the molten metal down her gullet. ‘WossamaNer?! Lost yer taste fer drink?’ Within seconds she was silenced by the lethal heat of the draught burning out her throat and her voice. It was scarcely slowed as it hit her stomach and seared her innards to a stinking crisp. The waves of pain pounded through her being, mounting in a rapid crescendo as the ﬂesh burned oﬀ her bones.  She felt the merciful blackness of unconsciousness rising in the wake of pain, but, as is the curse of all those condemned to such hells as these, no sooner had the bliss of oblivion been promised than she was wide awake and her body had been made quite whole again, ripe for torture once more.   * * * The reek of singed ﬂesh and smouldering hair was everywhere, blended with the fume of burning hoof. The stench bit the nostrils and so, even though every hot breath was gasped for, when it entered it chewed her nose and left her wincing.  Streams of molten copper swung lazily through the land around her; she had no memory of rural riverbanks and darting dragonﬂies amid the reeds but something in her knew that the gentle wending curves of blazing orange and green bore a resonance of another world. chapters.title: Chapter 2:  Forbidden Fruit  don’t know, Krishna, it doesn’t feel right to me. It isn’t honest.’ Maggot’s brow furrowed around the rose-coloured circlet that she habitually wore. ‘I don’t like it at all, hiding away, in secret.’ ‘But Maggot, most people can’t see you anyway – you’re permanently hidden from almost everyone,’ Krishna glanced at his partner sideways, checking to see if his point had been convincing. It had not.   ‘If it’s not a secret, why have you not told the other monks about me? Why do you have to sneak away to spend time with me and make up excuses to fool the other monks and novices? You’re even proud of how clever your lies are. They can’t see me because I’m a kinnari, but they can see you and besides, whether they can see me or not, I’m sure they would not approve of a monk having a girlfriend.’  ‘But that’s just it!’ Krishna grinned, ‘Since you’re not a “girl” but a “celestial being” it’s not against the rules – at least I’m preNy sure it’s not – well, not for monks anyway. I’m only nineteen Rains old, so I’m not a full monk yet and I’ve never heard anyone say a novice should not have a partner who’s a deva.’ As he was saying this, he was aware that he had made sure that he had not told KhujjuNara about his relationship with Maggot. She was a much respected lay follower of the Buddha, and a friend of Krishna, but she had no abilities to see devas and Krishna had not wanted to risk her disapproval. On account of this he had ‘neglected to mention to her’ this partnership with Maggot. His other elder mentor, the ragged monk Dusaka, who was from some remotely related spiritual tradition, seemed to be aware already that Krishna and Maggot were lovers but for his own reasons had not scowled at or scolded them for this. He was always diﬃcult to read and could never be second-guessed.  ‘Well that’s not a surprise,’ she grumbled, continuing to be unimpressed, ‘how often does the subject come up in an average conversation? And isn’t the monastic life based on “brahmacariya” – everyone in the monastery living as brothers and sisters and not having husbands, wives, partners?’  ‘You know, Maggot,’ Krishna, fully determined to push his point, now tried a diﬀerent angle of aNack, ‘there’s this theory about the word “brahmacariya”– it can mean “divine conduct” and they like to translate that as “celibacy”, no love-partners and so on, but it also means “walking with the gods” or “going with the holy ones” – don’t you see? You are one of the divine ones, you are a goddess, so if I “go” with you, I am in fact following the “brahmacariya”. It’s right there in the word.’  ‘So, why do you have to pretend to the other monks that you are doing other things when we are spending time together – I don’t get it.’   ‘Well, it’s a philosophical problem,’ he looked at Maggot sideways again, testing the eﬀect of this proclamation.

chapters.title: CHAPTER 3:  THE STOLEN CHILD  ou haven’t shaved your head yet,’ remarked Ananda. ‘Wha…?’ responded Krishna, surprised to see the Elder coming down the path, at this back part of the monastery woods. ‘It’s the full moon – look – the sun is setting there in the west and the moon is rising in the east. By the time it’s above the forest we should be at the hall for the Recitation.’   Krishna realized he had completely forgoNen this fortnightly head-shaving but he could not reveal to Ananda that it was because he was taken up with caring for Maggot and the new baby. That was out of the question.   ‘Oh, right!’ He blustered, ‘I’ll do that before dawn tomorrow.’  ‘And,’ Ananda continued, giving Krishna a somewhat studied sideways glance, ‘as it’s the Komudi full moon, this makes it your birthday; if I remember correctly. And isn’t your proper name Komudi – that no one ever uses – on account of you being born on this day?’  ‘You remember everything!’ the impressed Krishna retorted.   ‘Perhaps not everything,’ Ananda smiled, ‘but a lot.’ He was arranging his robe over his shoulder as they spoke. ‘And, as this is your twentieth, you could request full ordination and become a monk today – a fully ﬂedged bhikkhu.’ He repeated the slightly loaded side-glance, checking Krishna for his reaction to this thinly-veiled hint. ‘Since the Master is here in the Ghositarama, if you were to request the Full Acceptance today, it could be a very short and simple ceremony; he just says, ‘Ehi bhikkhu’ and it’s done.’   ‘That would be a great honour, as well as being really convenient,’ Krishna replied, his mind now racing to calculate how long all of these unexpected (at least for him) ceremonies would take. He was now in a dilemma, torn between loyalties, as he had promised Maggot that he would take care of the baby for the night whilst she went to visit her parents over in the Simsapa grove, outside the city of Kosambi. He wondered if he had time to ask Bee or Ant, or Gumbiya to take a message to her, or to ﬁll in for him, or if it would all be over quickly so he could get back while Tambaka was still resting peacefully, as she had just dropped oﬀ to sleep before Ananda had appeared.  ‘What should I do?!’ His mind raced. Not being risk-averse he decided to gamble on the baby sleeping peacefully for the next hour – hidden away in their nest in the deep thicket – so he said, ‘Let me get my robe from my kuti and we’ll ask if I can be ordained this evening – that will be a great opportunity. Let’s do it!’  Ever since Krishna had joined the Sangha as a novice, after the tragic and dramatic deaths of his two sisters, Amba and Tamba (laNerly known as Queen Samavati and Queen Magandiya) the kindly Ananda had taken him under his wing,

chapters.title: CHAPTER 5: THE UNINSPIRING MONK  o, what did you make of all that?’ Krishna had returned to his kuti after the communal meal and had invited his friend Surama, an Elder amongst the community of monks, to come along and continue the conversation they had begun, once the Master had departed, after he had given some forthright instruction to the community.  ‘Well,’ responded Krishna, ‘I had hoped to ask him if he could use his powers to tell me where Tambaka had disappeared to but, since he was mainly addressing Udayin about how misguided he had been with those brahmin visitors, I didn’t feel it was the right time. He even laid down a new, serious rule about not coming into contact with the opposite sex, with lustful intent, and he gave Udayin the full “Mogha purisa!” treatment – “Oh foolish man!” If I had asked him about Tambaka he would almost certainly have enquired if she was a relative, or how she was known to me; then what would I say? It wouldn’t be a good subject to raise in public.’ ‘Good point,’ Surama replied, ‘you were best oﬀ keeping a low proﬁle.’ He saw that Krishna was looking fraught and unseNled so he continued, ‘You know that I agree with you about how the Buddha has to keep up a front for the sake of the public, and that in its essence the teaching he espouses is a lot more broad and accommodating. ‘In his usual way of speaking, about the Middle Way, he says how happiness cannot come from pursuing sense pleasure as you will always want more. When the thrill is gone you just desire something else to replace it. That is one extreme.  ‘Then the other extreme is to try to supress all desires, to annihilate them, but that is doomed to failure as life keeps producing more things to want. No maNer how hard we try.  ‘He says the Middle Way is “to let go of desire” but I agree with you that that’s just the version for the masses. Really, how could that work? If I want something, if I need something and I “let go of the desire” there is still something missing, as far as I can see – you didn’t get the thing you needed and wanted, so surely you are still lacking that – no?’ ‘Absolutely, that just how I see it,’ said Krishna.  ‘So,’ Surama continued, ‘I feel it’s our duty as living beings to fulﬁl as many of those needs and wishes as possible, to honour the potential of our lives, and then to let go of aNachment to the pleasure we feel. This is the advanced path that the Master is encouraging but that he can’t speak about publicly as it would look like he was an indulgent and less-than-admirable teacher. We should not use the scanty virtue and meagre wisdom of the narrow-minded to measure the vast sagacity and compassion of the Buddha!

chapters.title: CHAPTER 6:  THE ENCOUNTER AT THE WELL   ife in Kulluta had become increasingly stressful and precarious over the last fifteen years. Sugandhi had been blissfully happy for the first year, after Harita was born, and even Mata-ji had been reasonably benign, but when her little girl reached the completion of one Rains the broad hints and out-right demands – ‘Now it’s time for a son!’ – began to mount. It was a mild irritation at first, and Sugandhi was otherwise very content with her new life, away from the gruesome duties and stench of her father’s slaughtering yard.  In time however, year by year, the stress mounted and was openly talked about as ‘the family problem’. No more babies came – girl or boy – no maNer what lengths they went in choosing auspicious days, fertility potions, spells by local shamans and seers of both genders. It didn’t help that, at least to Sugandhi’s eyes, her daughter might not have inherited her suspected father’s blue-black skin but the set of her features, her ink-black hair and the big dark purple eyes bore a striking resemblance to Krishna’s. Thankfully no-one else seemed to have made note of this but the growing resemblance was a worry.  When Harita turned six Rains the momentum of concern, as repeatedly voiced by Mata-ji, led to a new marriage being arranged for Jayanta. ‘Since you haven’t been able to give my son any more children, other than this girl,’ Mata-ji managing to both sneer and scowl simultaneously, ‘we have arranged that my son will take another bride.’ There was no discussion between Sugandhi and Jayanta on this, his parents had decided.  It had always puzzled Sugandhi why so many women only wanted sons and seemed biased against their own sex. She adored her girl and, now that she was six Rains, she was a friendly and helpful companion around the house and shared the village duties with the other womenfolk, both young and old.  The new bride was found, coming from a family of many children and, this time from the same caste as the Headman and Mata-ji, even a liNle bit more upscale in the social hierarchy. She seemed a nice enough girl, and when Jayanta eventually got round to talking with Sugandhi about it, he was quite apologetic and asked for her understanding about how diﬀerent things would be. She was touched by this gesture as it was plain he had had no choice in the maNer – Mata-ji had pressed the issue and her husband was also keen for a grandson from Jayanta. Their other children were all daughters, who now lived in their new family homes, three of them away and only one who still resided in Kulluta. chapters.title: CHAPTER 7:  MATANGA’S DEVOTION    ’y think they will le’ me travel with you?’ Matanga anxiously asked. ‘Oi’ll walk far behoind and not cross nobody’s shadow nor touch no food Oi’m not supposted to.’ She glanced up from having tried to keep her eyes downcast, as was expected of the lower menials, and for a moment looked directly at Ananda’s face, meeting his gaze.  ‘Once again, friend,’ Ananda began, ‘for those who follow the Way of the Buddha, concerns of caste and rank are put aside. For lay disciples, when they are in their own homes, they will observe the customs and duties of their position in society – like King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika of Kosala – but when they are visiting a monastery, or in the company of nuns or monks, they conduct themselves as humble lay-devotees, upasika and upasaka, and will respectfully converse with and share the food of all other disciples, whether nobles or farmers or candalas like you.’ ‘Is ’at true?!’ Matanga was amazed – firstly that Ananda had called her ‘friend’ but even more at this strange philosophy. ‘If the teaching of this Buddha can bring about such a change in people, such a diff’rent way of bein’, I definitely wan’ ter meet ’im. So does this mean Oi can come with you? With all of you, Oi mean.’ Matanga’s face flushed a little at having let it slip that she mostly wanted just to be close to Ananda but, her complexion having been sun-darkened by so much work in the outdoors and from rough living generally, it was hardly discernible; besides, Ananda was used to being attractive to people as he was so genial and easy to get along with, he was also a handsome man although by now well into his middle years.  ‘Yes, I think you can come with us,’ Ananda reassured her. ‘There are about sixty monks in our group but there are also a few laywomen and laymen walking with us to help with any needs along the way. You should be able to join with them but I will check with the other members of the Sangha, just so that people will know who you are and out of politeness to the group.’  ‘Thank you! Thank you!’ Matanga stopped trying to look at the ground and smiled up at Ananda, her eyes locking onto his. ‘You are truly the koindest person Oi’ve ever met – thank you again! Oi’ll just go and collect moy bundle and Oi’ll find you all at the forest, and Oi’ll ’ope that no one objects to me comin’ along.’   * * *  To her great relief there were no complaints about the idea of her joining the troupe of lay disciples and she soon got into the rhythm of the road. They left the village, which sat between the River Gomati and the River Sarayu, after the Sangha had walked through it for alms in the early morning. She was glad to be on the road

chapters.title: CHAPTER 8: KAPILAVATTHU –  THE CITADEL OF THE SAKYANS    ing Pasenadi was feeling torn. He deeply loved his queen, Mallika, but in all their years of marriage she had only borne him one daughter, the Princess Vajiri. She, in turn, he loved very much but she was not a male, and according to the laws and customs of the warrior-noble kshatriyans, only a son born to the anointed king and his queen could inherit the throne of Kosala. If he died without a legitimate son to inherit, it would inevitably fall to bloody disputes between nephews, cousins and boys that had been born from liaisons outside the royal marriage.  One such was Prince Jeta, who was a fine young fellow, and a wealthy and well-regarded personage in Savatthi. He had sold the park he owned outside of town to Anathapindika so that he in turn could gift it to the Sangha. He had not only made a fortune from that but he had had his name enshrined in the minds of the manyfold disciples of the Master since, through no wish of his own, the monastery had become known to one and all as the Jetavana – Jeta’s Grove. If he had been the son of Queen Mallika, all would be simple, however his mother was one of King Pasenadi’s concubines, the kshatriyan Lady Varshika, a minor princess, descended from a fourth son of his great-grandfather. All of this meant he would need to find another wife and to put her on an equal footing with Queen Mallika, and then hope that this new bride would provide him with the wished-for princely son. It was a worry.  Part of what he dreaded was the need to inform Queen Mallika for he wished always to respect her and, publicly as well as he did privately, demonstrate that he held her in the highest regard. She had come from a humble background and had only been the daughter of the chief garland-maker of Savatthi before King Pasenadi chanced to meet her and had fallen immediately in love, both marrying her and anointing her as Queen that very same day. There had been grumblings that she was a commoner but the King had always come to her defence, asserting his power as an absolute monarch to raise her up to His Royal Level.  When he finally brought the issue to her attention he was taken aback by her responding with the words, ‘I was wondering when you would realize that this was going to be a necessity. One slip would be enough to cause disaster; even though she was quick enough to make excuses, there were reasons and there were reasons why she might get something wrong. To use some northern vernacular term, or using the kitchen way of counting by numbering her finger joints, might be something she could get away with, but to pick something up with her left hand, when a kshatriya would never use anything but their right, would bring the edifice of pretence crashing down.  Prince Mahanama was relieved that the palace coffers would not have to provide a dowry which, for a Royal Wedding, could be ruinously expensive. The cost of hosting King Pasenadi and the Kosalan embassy for over a Moon had already drained the resources of himself and many of the noble houses. One aspect he was still concerned about was how to sustain the integrity of the deception over time. A number of nights had passed in fretful sleeplessness, trying to consider who to send with ‘the Princess’ and how secrecy could be maintained in Vasabha’s court, especially if she had the customary crowd of supposed relatives and familiar servants from home around her:– This really is a problem! People talk, and make new friends. How can it all be arranged to prevent the risk of slippage? And how are the Sakyan monks in Savatthi now to be encouraged to accept the invitations they were declining? To his surprise it was in an unguarded moment when, happening to see Vasabha being adjusted in her newest sarong and jeweled kamarband by Kesini, it came to him like a perfectly formed and well-wrapped package. He saw how he could send her with just one reliable servant and yet make it seem like this was a sign of great virtue and faith in the King, and in the security of Vasabha’s prospective new life in Savatthi.  It was the suspicious and supercilious glances that both Lady Jantu and Lady Piya gave Kesini as they helped Vasabha with her accoutrements that had given him the cue. The girl had just one hand, having lost the other in a tragic fire, and moreover she was from Kosambi in Vamsa, to the far south. The actual wedding was conducted by brahmin priests since the monks and nuns were prohibited from performing marriages by their Rule. This other ceremony was a blessing by the Sangha to wish them well as a couple and to invoke as many benevolent forces as possible – from all around the cakkavala, the universal system – and to encourage the kindly, noble, unselfish aspects of the heart within to be strengthened and to bless their union as well. It was going to be another test of her adaptability and resourcefulness as this was a further item that had not made it on to the list of ‘essentials’.  ‘I’m so glad you’re going to meet the Buddha, Miss,’ Kesini was quite excited. ‘I had the chance to go to his monastery in Kosambi a few times, with Gavinna who I looked after. She was a concubine of King Udena’s grandfather and had been put out to pasture long ago. She was very old and completely blind but she saw everything – if you know what I mean. She could tell exactly what was going on in people’s minds just by the sound and feel of their walk or the tone of their voice. She had visions too that she would tell me about sometimes.  ‘Anyway, when we had the opportunity, and when the Master was in the King’s good books, we’d go to listen to his talks. It was wonderful.’ ‘How would the Buddha not be in the King’s favour?’ Vasabha took care to use her posh voice at all times, even when it was apparently just her and Kesini in her chambers. You never knew when someone might be eavesdropping or just coming up to a doorway, many of which were only equipped with a curtain rather than a wooden door.  ‘Uhh! King Udena blew hot and cold all the time. You never could keep track of his moods. One Moon we’re all to go with him, in full pomp and with armloads of offerings, to pay respects to the Master and listen to his teaching, then two Moons later he’s lost faith again and he’s banned any of the court from going near the Ghositarama. chapters.title: CHAPTER 11: ‘TOGETHER FOREVER’   hy are you doing all this for us?’ Maggot asked Muñca before he made his preparations to get them all to the Tusita Heaven, ‘The Abode of the Contented’. Her grief-torn concerns about Tambaka had been punctuated more and more by this question over the last hours. ‘You are giving us all this time and attention, you’ve risked your own safety in the Underworld, and now perhaps the wrath of the kidnappers if you help us find my daughter – what makes this so important to you?’ ‘It’s simple, really, I didn’t spell it out before but the main reason I hold you and your friends in such high esteem is on account of the way you helped me and my dear ones. As you might be aware, musicians are often fond of their drugs – not just in the Human Realm and amongst the Earth Spirits but amongst the gandharvas too – and when they have made what they feel is their finest music under the influence, it makes it even harder to give up than an ordinary addiction,’ Muñca looked pained as he spoke of this, as if a cataract of bad memories were washing through him.  ‘A number of my family members got thoroughly hooked on amatagandha and their lives have been sad and painful since. Some have died, some have almost wasted away altogether. This is also why I think that Miss Sugandha, your friend Ant’s, supposition that some gandharvas might be involved in the abduction of your daughter is correct. It’s a grim thought to entertain, but they might be helping not just for spite and vengeance but also to get their hands on whatever diminishing supplies of the perfume might remain.’  Muñca seemed to be enduring this heart-breaking situation well and his story touched Maggot, and the others who were listening in. He paused and said, ‘So that’s the sad story but it’s what motivates me to help and to risk my comfort and safety.’ Maggot’s sombre mood was lifted a little by this impressive display of courage and unselfishness. For a while she brightened up and her countenance matched the iridescent pink and rose-adorned hues of her robes.   * * *   As they tidied their things and bid their farewells to Samuddaja and Irandati, and the other nagas of the household, Bee took a moment to check in on Ant, now alone after Ninka’s sudden departure. Ant was often very quiet, and kept her moods to herself but Bee knew that she felt things very strongly.  ‘How are you doing?’

chapters.title: CHAPTER 12: A KANAVERA FALLS   inka felt as though something within her was fading, becoming thinner, paler. The vibrant and colourful dances continued around her, the waves of exquisite perfume ebbed and flowed, yet she felt a dimming, a diminution, a strange dampness and sense of dross edging in around her, dulling the gleeful delights of the party.  There was a banquet of exotic foods laid out for all the revellers, the rich aromas mingling with the scents exuded by the devas and the accharas, as well as with the fragrances of the celestial flowers – mandarava and mañjusaka – it was a feast, a delight to the eye and to the sense of smell, but Ninka found herself turning away. All this bounty, this joyful play, palled and lost its glamour.  She was seated beside her betrothed, the deva prince she was soon to be wed to but, perhaps affected by the waning of her interest in all around them, he had been ignoring her and was deep in rapturous conversation with a deva to his left, a jewel-bedecked beauty whose eyes shone with fascination and delight at Malabhari’s every word. She was entranced by him. The prince was equally fixated on her so Ninka scarcely had to say, ‘Please excuse me,’ before she drifted quietly away.  The dancing and the party-games, the absorption in the food and drink, were undisturbed by Ninka’s departure. Quietly she floated beyond the edge of the glade; she had had nothing to eat, after the token sip of nectar she had had to take at Malabhari’s bidding.  In the shade of the trees across the lotus pond Ninka noticed that her gossamer robes seemed more sombre in tone than they usually did. She moved her arm out into the full sunlight of the morning yet, even there, the blues and purples were definitely less rich, the edges almost grey. As she moved her hands around, picking up different pieces of the fabrics she was wearing to look at them more closely, she felt a strange stickiness in her armpits. ‘What is this?’ she wondered, reaching to test the sensation with her fingers. Not only did a faintly rank tang strike her nose but she saw flakes of skin, a dusty slough, gathered on the tips.  ‘I am fading indeed,’ she realized, ‘and there’s nothing I can do about it.’ She had not had any food when with the nagas, having lost her appetite and she knew that having not eaten for some time, the signs she was now experiencing meant that the deva-life she had lived for so long was coming to an end. Her hands and feet now hurt and she could see that she no longer had the radiance, the aura that would, in the past, have easily dispelled the shadows beneath the circle of trees beside the pond where she was sitting.  A wave of tiredness washed over her but she felt restless, agitated at the same time. She curled her legs beneath her and leant against the trunk of one of the trees,

chapters.title: CHAPTER 13: THE GROUP OF SIX  uite soon after Krishna had arrived at the Jetavana he had renewed his friendship with Khujjuttara and that connection had developed helpfully over time. He had been somewhat sobered, chastened by the painful consequences of what he and the other monks had got up to in Kitagiri, so he was now much more motivated by caring and compassion, and an appreciation of the consequences of the choices that he made. He was still thoroughly convinced of the value and validity of his ‘Sooner! More!’ philosophy of life-affirmation but he was now much more discerning and thoughtful about the impact that his words and actions, and those of the people around him, had upon the world. In this light he was very grateful for the company of Ananda and Khujjuttara and her young helper, Matanga. They were a good influence upon him, he felt, and he was glad of their always practical and sage advice, and their example of modesty and kindness.  Since the Buddha spent most of his time these days at the Jetavana, and since Ananda was his chief attendant, it often came about that he was not available for a chat with Krishna, to offer his counsel and companionship. This led to Krishna regularly sitting with Khujjuttara and Matanga, chatting in the sala or under the trees, and spending many hours of the day in their company. He felt that this was all very innocent; Khujjuttara was, after all a white-haired Elder, and Matanga was pointedly restrained and properly behaved. Certainly she was young and pretty but she was modest to a fault and never roused any flirtatious feelings in the monks or laymen that drew close to her sagacious charge, when they came to Khujjuttara for advice or to be reminded of various passages of the Teachings that she was well-versed in.  It was now a Moon or two after Krishna had arrived from Kitagiri and he was getting very comfortable with this new routine and circle of friends, when his old companion, Surama, walked into the monastery. He had moved on from Kitagiri a dozen years before and Krishna had not seen him since.  ‘Hello, old friend!’ Krishna was very excited to meet him after such a long absence. ‘Where have you been all this time? I’ve not heard a word about you from anyone who came to Kitagiri, or here either, for that matter. What have you been up to? Where have you been living? You look well.’ Surama gave a cursory nod to the two women that Krishna had been talking with, when he had walked up to them, and made it clear to Krishna that it would indeed be good to catch up. With another derogatory glance at Krishna’s companions, he suggested, ‘Let’s go to your kuti, or somewhere quiet, so we can have a proper talk.’

chapters.title: CHAPTER 19: PUJIKA’S DELIGHT  ujika had moved to a small village, called Katara, to the south of Savatthi, on the occasion of her marriage. She had been very happy about this for, even though she was leaving her family home, this village of her husband was even closer to the Jetavana than the city of Savatthi. It was a fine little place to raise their growing family and it meant that she could easily visit the Jetavana every day, even with her three little boys and her expanded belly. One of her delights was, in the hour before dawn, to rise before the rest of the family, sometimes with her third boy on her hip, and go to the village Assembly Hall to tidy it up and to prepare for possible visitors. Katara was of modest size but, because so many folk would come from far and wide to visit the Jetavana, and would need a place to find and purchase offerings to take to the Master and the Sangha, they were quite prosperous there. The Hall was a finely built shelter where the village council would meet but – and more importantly for Pujika – it was also the place where Elders from the Sangha, (usually the monks rather than the nuns since the monastery of the female community was close to the walls of Savatthi) would sometimes come to sit and receive alms.  Katara was only three or four bow-shots from the gates of the Jetavana so, when any of the agèd or infirm Sangha members wanted to go on the alms-round, or if there was a special occasion in the village such as a marriage or a baby blessing, they would use the Hall of Assembly as a place to gather. On very rare and wonderful days the Master would take this shorter route and come to Katara village himself and stop a while at the Hall.  Pujika had made it her daily custom to sweep the Hall as the light came back into the world, to shake out the mats and set them straight, and to fill the jugs with fresh water. The place was close to her home and the garland workshop, and it would put her heart at ease to know that, should any of the Sangha, on their early morning alms-round, need to stop and rest, the place was always ready. She would customarily bring some flowers to deck the seats and shrine as votive offerings, often draping these around the neck of her snoozing child as she made her way there. On the special days when an event was planned, if they knew the Elders were going to receive an offering there or if the nuns or monks were going to perform a blessing, she would be extra diligent and make abundant flower offerings, to add to those of other devotees.  As time had gone by images had appeared in her mind of celestial beings, wreathed in flowers and smiling at her, most often one bright round face clad all in the reds of the kanavera.

chapters.title: CHAPTER 20:  PRINCE VIDUDABHA VISITS  HIS ANCESTRAL HOME   idudhabha had been pestering his mother, and occasionally his father, since he was seven Rains old. He had seen that the other children of the royal household – his half-sister Princess Vajiri and the daughters and sons of the noble families of Kosala – all received presents from their maternal as well as their paternal grandparents whereas he never did. Toy horses, elephants, play-swords and shields, things he envied came to his companions in this way but not to him.  This was not to say that he was not showered with gifts from his royal father’s mother, and his great-grandmother who was still alive although very deaf and a little loose in thought, however these ‘women’s presents’ were not like the ones the other boys got from their grandfathers. King Pasenadi’s father, King Mahakosala, had passed away long ago, so Vidudabha had received no sharp jewelled daggers, or bows with a spring to make arrows go a decent distance, or any keen-pointed arrows for that matter. He was aggrieved.  Over and over again he would complain, ‘Mother, the other boys and girls get many presents from their maternal grandparents but I never do. Are you an orphan? Don’t you have a mother and father?’ Vasabha, who often found it hard to love her petulant and demanding, entitled son had become used to this appeal and always countered him with such as, ‘My dear, my parents are Sakyan royals and they live a long way off, below the Himavant, that’s why they never send you anything.’ The prince was not satisfied with this but it would end the issue, for a time.  When he reached the age of sixteen Rains his status had changed from that of a child to not just an adult but, in a show of confidence in his only royal born son, the King had appointed Prince Vidudabha as commander-in-chief of the army as well.  The Prince was no longer so interested in boyish presents from grandparents – he had plentiful supplies of all the clothes, weapons and ornaments that an heir to the throne of the great kingdom of Kosala could wish for – but he was eager to go out into the world and he was ever intrigued by the family of his royal mother:– Why do they never visit? Why had they never even sent any messages? Weren’t they the family of the Buddha himself? Why were visits from the Sakyan royal family never made? Other folk from the north came by – Koliyans, Sakyans and Kullutans – so the journey could not be so arduous, so why never his grandfather, Prince Mahanama, and his grandmother, the Princess Maddarupi? It was mysterious.

Ant and Ninka had been locked in an intense conversation before the newly-arrived deva had joined them. Ant tried to bear in mind that her belovèd had just been hatched into this new life but she was aggrieved and sick at heart, ireful too. The beauty of their surroundings was lost to them.  ‘How is it that you didn’t recognize Muñca when he first appeared? The princesses said he was notorious in this, their realm – the devas in the Realm of the Guardians had said nothing but, for all of you here in the Thirty-Three, it sounds like he’s infamous,’ Ant pressed her.  Ninka looked up into her face and could not speak at first.  ‘Did you recognize him?’ Ant was doing her best to read Ninka’s expression, now tear-stained as it was. Her heart sank. ‘You did know. You knew all along. How could you?’ Ant was aghast, feeling a storm of emotion. ‘Why?!?’ A righteous rage flashed through her. ‘Poor Maggot! And the rest of us tagging along, with the nagas and the yakkhas, and all the way up to the Tusita – you let him drag us all behind him on a wild goose chase,’ her words slowed down and softened as she took in Ninka’s sweet face now twisted with tears and anguish. A weeping deva is a wrenching sight to see. A realization began to dawn in Ant’s heart, ‘It was…’ Ninka wiped her eyes, ‘For you, it was that I could not bear to be parted from you. A day at a pointless party in the Nandana Grove and decades will go by in the Realm of Humans, for you in the Realm of Earth-spirits too.’ She took a breath, letting the vitality of the airs of her home clear her head a little.  ‘I confess, and I ask your forgiveness – and of everyone of our friends, especially Maggot – I thought that I knew who he was as soon as he appeared in the Underworld. When he whisked us out of there I was certain, then it all came crashing in. chapters.title: CHAPTER 24: REUNIONS   very tongue was wagging in Savatthi. The stories of the massacre of the Sakyans – the Master’s own people – as well as the demise of virtually the entirety of the Kosalan army, had reached the city with great speed. Bad news travels fast.  People had been generally unhappy about the way that Vidudabha had seized power. Even though his father, King Pasenadi, had made some grievous mistakes, such as the wiping out of General Bandhula’s family so recently, he had been regarded as a good and just king. He was a sincere and dedicated disciple of the Master and always displayed the most genuine humility and friendship towards him, and to his monks and nuns. He had been beloved by the populace, his only shortcoming in the eyes of most people had been his failure to produce more than a couple of children. Princess Vajiri and now the late King Vidudabha were his only offspring, either through formal or casual liaisons. Now that Vidu the Fay was gone, and it was well known that the old King had passed away near Rajagaha, the big question of the day – along with the issues of funerals and inheritances for many of the noble houses of Kosala – was ‘who will ascend the throne of the kingdom, since both legitimate kings have passed away?’ It was a sad time for all. It seemed that a majority of the families of Savatthi, whether humble or noble, had lost at least one man in the army that was washed down the Aciravati, as well as many women who were in the waggon train and cook-tents. Hardly anyone had any physical remains of their loved ones that could be properly cremated, however, so there was an endless succession of bodiless funeral ceremonies and memorials held in the burning grounds outside the city and on the river’s banks, and at the local shrines.  The lamentations and mourning for the Sakyan people also filled the air. Yes, they had caused offence by foisting a low-caste bride upon the King, and that subterfuge had been maintained for many years, but Queen Vasabha was well-liked regardless. It was now suspected that her genuine ‘common touch’, and ability to relate comfortably and helpfully with the poor-folk, was a result of her own humble origins, like those of the equally appreciated Queen Mallika.  In the search for a new ruler it was appreciated that King Pasenadi had had a number of other, so-called ‘minor wives’. There were Ubbiri, Soma and Sakula (some male relatives of whom were considered), and Vimala who was a sister of King Bimbisara. chapters.title: CHAPTER 25: LONE WANDERINGS  lose to the city of Savatthi it may have been, but the world inside the Eastern Gatehouse Monastery was a place apart.  Vasabha and Kesini settled into their new life feeling a strange buoyancy and delight, not despite but rather because of their changed circumstances. The loss of status, from Queen to new and junior lay woman, from King’s Mother to monastery helper, was a massive relief to Vasabha, in contrast to what some around her expected. The nuns, novices and other lay helpers, and aspirants to the monastic life, were steadily impressed, as the days and Moons went by, that Vasabha and her one-handed companion were cheerfully ready to be part of the community in a heartful way and were happy to pick up any chores and tasks asked of them, sometimes even the grubbier the better.  The great joy they both experienced was from two sources. Firstly, the bliss of not having to pretend anything to anyone, even to the extent of mentioning that Vasabha was prone to smelling fragrant not because she was wearing perfume and thereby breaking one of the Precepts, but because her mother was a kinnari. She wore this attribute quite casually and, when some doubted it, she was grateful that the Arahant, Sister Uppalavanna, assured others that this was no new deception of Vasabha but was the reality. She could know this directly by being able to see Maggot and Ambaka often around Vasabha and Kesini, and the great Elder had regularly chatted with them herself as well.  Kesini was also quite open about the absence of her hand and, in a similar vein, she would sometimes jokingly mention that the cause of its loss was the very friend she had been serving for the last twenty years, since it was Magandiya that had set the plan for the burning of the seraglio in place, and that this had been Vasabha in an existence a lifetime or two previously. Accordingly, Vasabha might blush or look sheepish at the reminder but Kesini’s bold good humour was clearly sincere around such memories – she had no hard feelings, resentments concerning the condition she had been living with all these years. She would often say on this, ‘Being one-handed makes you mindful and sharpens your wits. You have to think things through and take nothing for granted, and it also reminds you that life is very uncertain and undependable. You should try it sometime!’ She would chuckle. chapters.title: CHAPTER 26: ON THE WESTERN SHORE  ammu, Swami-ji! Here Jammu,’ the village children had crowded around Krishna, this stranger with a weird accent, and who was so black and white. His beard was now long and the colour of fresh snow, his skin had weathered to a wrinkled but still soot-black sheen.  Krishna had emerged from the forest, after having ambled his way through the open stretches but, more often, having clambered through tangled thickets, and had entered this village in the early morn. The journey thus far had taken him several Moons, without the blessing of Dusaka and Tingri’s guidance.  The children excitedly showered him with questions but most of it was lost on Krishna. He was struggling to understand the dialect and there were half a dozen voices chirping at once.  ‘Taxila?’ He questioned, gesticulating to the west, the south and the east. ‘Do you know where I should go to reach Taxila?’ The smallest boy, eager to be heard in the gaggle of voices, spoke up loudly, and with authority, stepping to the front, to declare, ‘Jammu!’ He pointed in all directions with a grubby finger, ‘This all Jammu! Not Taxila,’ he felt proud to have made that clear to this wandering holy man who had just emerged from the forest.  A taller, quiet girl stepped forward from the rear of the group of friends, put her hands on the little one’s shoulders and spoke, in slow and clear words, ‘Taxila, big city, south, not here, River Vitasta – follow Vitasta – to walk, many days. People here, go there,’ she pointed to the ground and the stone-built houses around them layered with wooden timbers, and the smaller wooden shacks. ‘Taxila south, there.’ The sun was now well-risen to their left and she pointed firmly to the downslope of the hill ahead. ‘Thank you!’ Krishna was relieved to have now oriented himself. He then stood and indicated his iron alms-bowl, which he had maintained with great care all these years, and made the universal gesture of pointing to his mouth. The new day had brought with it the old feeling of an empty stomach.  The children immediately understood and he was grabbed by several of them, being invited to homes in a number of different directions. By gesturing with his walking fingers he indicated he would make a circuit of the homes and people could offer something if they wanted to.  His alms-round was not very quiet as the gathering of keyed up youngsters had expanded as word of the agèd and unusual visitor had spread. A few adults had joined them too, one of them apparently being the village headman as he spoke to welcome Krishna and to show him, mostly by gesture and beckoning, the best way to walk around the village pathways. chapters.title: Chapter 2: Forbidden Fruit  1) p8:– I’m a kinnari: Kinnari are a class of earth-devas. They feature extensively in Mara and the Mangala I: The Killer   2) ibid:– it’s not against the rules – at least I’m pretty sure it’s not: Eventually the Buddha did establish this detail of the Vinaya rule entailing ‘defeat’ for a monk, i.e. ‘now at that time a certain monk indulged in sexual intercourse with a female naga… a yakkhini… this is an o#ence involving defeat’ (Book of the Discipline I, pp57-8); also, it is the same ‘whether it is a young female naga or a kinnari’ (N1, VA 279-ThigA 225). These are the subclauses of Defeat Rule 1.   3) p9:– that is what society expects: A philosophy similar to that expounded by Krishna’s father Kamanita, as recounted in The Pilgrim Kamanita in Ch. 20: ‘The Unreasonable Child’; especially on p120.  4) ibid:– that urge towards enlightenment, is the life-pulse of the universe: This passage is adapted from D.T. Suzuki, Essays in Zen Buddhism I, p75, quoted in Silent Rain, p86, note 1, and in Rain on the Nile, p196, note 21.   5) ibid:– ‘Jambu’. It’s even there in what you are called: The word ‘jambu’ is indeed the classical term for the ‘rose-apple’ as in the ancient name for the Indian sub-continent ‘Jambudvīpa’ (Skt) or ‘Jambudīpa’ (Pāli), ‘the Land of Rose-Apples’. The formal name for the tree is Syzygium jambos.   6) ibid:–  it’s what we call ‘skilful means’, as it has a noble cause in mind: The Pali for this is upāya. In the Southern Buddhist literature the Buddha never tells any outright lies for any reason but he does occasionally allow himself to be misunderstood, without correcting the wrong assumption. This is a major theme of The Pilgrim Kamanita and is exempli%ed on p121 and in note 18 to Ch. 20, pp306-7 (ibid). In the Northern School, outright lies seems to be sanctioned, as in the ‘burning house’ story in the Lotus Sutra.   7) p10:– soon we’ll have a hatchling to think of as well: As described later, kinnaris lay eggs and are thus known as ‘twice-born’. Although in the Pali Canon they are described as human-like in form and occasionally living as a couple with a human spouse, and having children together (for example, in Jāt 546, the hermit Vaccha and the kinnari Rahavatī and their children) they are sometimes represented iconographically as having a human torso and bird’s legs, and wings attached to their hips. This is plainly a misreading of the texts and an incorrect representation.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: ‘To Ful%l Desire is Happiness’  1) p23:– If you weren’t a monk it wouldn’t be a problem: Buddhist monastics abide by the precepts of not engaging in any kind of sexual activity, with any other beings or even with themselves. Celibacy is the rule for all, whether a novice or fully ordained.  For Buddhist lay people, the standard is to ‘refrain from sexual misconduct’, so sexual relations between consenting adults, where no one is being taken advantage of or deceived, are considered completely appropriate.   2) ibid:– when he was questioned about his views: This dialogue between the Buddha and Ariṭṭha is found at M 22 and it is also the basis of Pac #68 (Vin iv 134). This kind of inappropriate indulgence is also mentioned in the origin story and text of Saṅg #4, (Vin iv 1-2); this was laid down based on the actions of Bhikkhu Udāyin. ‘Should any bhikkhu, lustful, with perverted thoughts, speak in a woman’s presence in praise of ministering to his own sensuality, inviting sexual intercourse thus, “Sister, the highest kind of ministering is this, namely, ministering with this (sexual) act to a virtuous lofty-natured observer of the Brahmacariya such as I am”, this entails initial and subsequent meeting of the Sangha,’ (Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli trans.).  3) p24:– keep remembering ‘Sooner! More!’: As in Mara and the Mangala I, Ch. 15, p179.  4) ibid:– like the Holy Deva Dharani who rose up as a witness: One of the most popular legends around the Buddha’s enlightenment was that, when Māra’s army would not acknowledge defeat and Māra called his followers to be his witnesses to his claim to supremacy in the universe, the Bodhisattva reached down and touched the earth, to call the Earth Mother, Dharani, to be his witness and to vouch for his genuine supremacy. A version of this story is found in many late accounts of the Buddha’s life, such as the Buddhavaṃsa and the Lalitavisatara. A very readable account is found in Oriental Mythology, by Joseph Campbell, pp21–22.   5) ibid:– Didn’t he have a deva friend too?: As found at S 1.20  6) p25:– so they would have to squeeze by you: This incident involved Udāyin and was the basis for Saṅg #2 and #3, (Vin iii 119 and Vin iii 127).  7) ibid:– but Udayin too: As above, Udāyin was the cause of the establishment of numerous Vinaya rules, see for example Dictionary of Pali Proper Names, p376, §2.  8) ibid:– that is when the self realizes the highest Nirvana: This passage is found at D 1.3.20.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: The Encounter at the Well  1) p38:– all daughters, who now lived in their new family homes: It is still the custom in India for a newly-married couple to reside in the husband’s home.   2)         p39:– after extensive astrological research had been made: This echoes the process of %nding a new wife for Kamanita, in The Pilgrim Kamanita, Ch. 14, pp83-86.  3)         p40:– regular applications of madayantika: This is henna, or camphire, which is still used today in these regions of Northern India and Pakistan.   4)         p42:– he bowed three times: This is the traditional way of formally greeting elder monastics, in both the Southern and Northern traditions. chapters.title: Chapter 15: The Ambitions of Devadatta  1) p128:– Like the Buddha he had been a prince … uncle to … Rahula too: All this description of Devadatta is according to the Pali Canon.   2) p129:– Devadatta got up from his seat: The account of this challenge to the Buddha, and the suggestion by Devadatta that he take over the leadership of the Sangha, is found at CV 7.3.1 The Pali for ‘a gob of phlegm’ is ‘kheḷāpaka’. The original phrase the Buddha used in this exchange was ‘chavassa kheḷapakassa’ – ‘chava’ meaning ‘vile, low, miserable, wretched’. PTS Dic. p275.  3) p130:– There are five changes I wish to propose: These five are listed at CV 7.3.14-15. In the original text it is spelled out that Devadatta’s explicit intent in proposing these five changes was to create a rift, a schism in the Sangha. He was aware that austerity impresses the public so it would be a wedge to help break up the community.  Some of his co-conspirators were indeed named: Kokālikā, Katamorata-tissaka, Khandadevī-putta and Samudadatta.   4) ibid:– What qualities do you see in me: This passage is adapted from M 77.8-9, ‘The Greater Discourse to Sakuladāyin’.   5) p131:– Let those who wish to: This all comes from CV 7.3.15.  6) ibid:– However, there are attributes my disciples respect: This passage is paraphrased from M 77.10-38. The last of the categories listed (‘the ways to develop wholesome states’) is comprised of many subsections that the sutta describes in detail, such as: 1) The Four Foundations of Mindfulness; 2) The Four Right Kinds of Striving; 3) The Four Bases for Spiritual Power; 4) The Five Faculties; 5) The Five Powers; 6) The Seven Factors of Enlightenment; 7) The Noble Eightfold Path; 8) The Eight Liberations; 9) The Eight Bases for Transcendence; 10) The Ten Kasiṇas; 11) The Four Jhānas; 12) Insight Knowledge; 13) The Mind-made Body; 14) The Kinds of Supernormal Power; 15) The Divine Ear; 16) The Ability to Read the Minds of Others; 17) The Recollection of Past Lives; 18) The Divine Eye; 19) The Destruction of the Outflows (āsava).   7) p132:– Hiri and Siri, the asura sisters: These two played a significant role in Mara and the Mangala I , pp319-79. The Kalakanja-asura are mentioned at D 20.12; they are described as ‘terrible to see’. They are also described in The Three Worlds According to King Ruang, pp107-8. The parents of Hiri and Siri were Queen Sujā, an asura, and King Indra, a deva, so they were of mixed celestial ancestry. See also, Ch. 24, note 6 of Mara and the Mangala I.

chapters.title: Chapter 17: Scandal in Savatthi  1) p147:– The court was convened: It is clear that there were formal judicial procedures in the time of the Buddha and in those regions. For example, at Par #2 in the Bhikkhu Pāṭimokkā, court cases over property and objects are mentioned several times, see The Buddhist Monastic Code, Vol I, pp54, 64 & 72. In the Bhikkhuṇī Pāṭimokka the nuns are explicitly forbidden to launch a legal case against any householder or wanderer, this is Saṅg #1 in the Bhikkhuṇī Pāṭimokkā. Lastly, at A 10.176, it is mentioned that, ‘If called to a town meeting, a group meeting, a gathering of relatives, to a guild meeting or royalty, if asked as a witness, “come and tell what you know”: if they don’t know, they say “I don’t know”; if they know, they say, “I know”.’  2) p148:– dressing in an unadorned and modest fashion: The custom then, as now in the Southern Buddhist countries, is to wear white, or white and black, undecorated clothing when visiting monasteries or attending Dharma teaching events, such as retreats. Customarily the body is also kept covered, from neck to ankles and wrists, by such plain clothing in order to maintain modesty.   3) ibid:– within the monasteries … any caste, any station in life: In Buddhist monasteries, rank and social power are put aside. The illiterate villager might thus sit beside, or even in front of, a regional governor or a local wealthy matriarch. Not always(!) but often this is the case.   4) ibid:– Sukhavati: Means ‘The Abode of Happiness’.   5) ibid:– Sattuka and Kalidanta: Sattuka was the name of a bandit that was spotted on the way to his execution by the laywoman Bhadda-Kuṇḍalakesā – ‘Bhadda with curly hair’. She fell in love at that first sight of Sattuka and begged her father to bribe the guard and let her marry him. Sattuka later hatched the idea to take her jewels and push her off the Robber’s Cliff but, through quick thinking, she turned the tables and pushed him off instead. She became an Arahant nun eventually, being acknowledged (ironically) as ‘foremost in swift intuition’. Her story is found at Thig 107-11. ‘Kalidanta’ means ‘Black-tooth’.   6) p150:– The words would not come: Devadatta had already lost his previously extensive super-normal powers, as evidenced at CV 7.2.1: ‘As soon as the thought that “It is I who ought to lead the Bhikkhu-Sangha” arose in his mind, Devadatta was deprived of his psychic powers.’ So this blockage is more because of fear of his teacher than from Devadatta’s super-normal interference.

chapters.title: Chapter 25: Lone Wanderings  1) p243:– thereby breaking one of the Precepts: The seventh of the Eight Precepts is, ‘I undertake the Precept to refrain from entertainment, beautification and adornment’.
